{{short description|Lemma concerning the limit of subadditive sequences}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2026}}
In mathematics, and in particular in [[calculus]], '''Fekete's lemma''' (also called '''Fekete's subadditive lemma''') is a [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] concerning the [[limit (mathematics)|limit]] of [[Subadditivity|subadditive sequences]]. The lemma provides an estimate for the linear growth rate of such sequences.

The lemma is named after the Hungarian-Israeli mathematician [[Michael Fekete]], who proved it in 1923.<ref>{{cite book |title=Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Probability_Theory_and_Combinatorial_Opt/Nn23zej42tIC
 |publisher=SIAM |date=1 January 1997 |isbn=978-0-89871-380-0 |author=J. Michael Steele |language=en |page=3}}</ref>

== Statement of the theorem ==

In this article, <math>\N</math> denotes the [[natural number]]s. This set does not include the number 0.

A sequence of [[real number]]s <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> is called a '''subadditive sequence''' if and only if for all <math>m,n\in\N</math> one has

<math>a_{n+m}\le a_n+a_m.</math>

'''Fekete's lemma''' states that for every subadditive sequence,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}=\inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

That is, the sequence <math>\frac{a_n}{n}</math> converges to its [[infimum]]. Note that this infimum may be <math>-\infty</math>.

== Proof ==
To prove that the limit exists and equals the infimum, it suffices to show that

<math>\inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n},</math>

where <math>\liminf</math> and <math>\limsup</math> denote the [[limit inferior]] and [[limit superior]], respectively. The two left inequalities always hold, so it is enough to prove the rightmost inequality

<math>\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

Since the sequence is subadditive, one can prove by [[mathematical induction|induction]] that for all <math>m,n,l,k\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{nl+mk}\le na_l+ma_k.</math>

Define <math>a_0=0</math>. Then this inequality also holds when one of the indices <math>m,n,l,k</math> is 0.

Now fix some <math>q\in\N</math>. For every <math>n\in\N</math> there exist <math>m\in\N</math> and <math>0\le r\le q-1</math> such that <math>n=mq+r</math>. Hence, by the inequality above,

<math>a_n\le ma_q+a_r.</math>

Define <math>C_q=\max(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{q-1})</math>. Dividing the inequality above by <math>n</math> yields

<math>\frac{a_n}{n}\le \frac{ma_q+a_r}{n}
= \frac{ma_q}{n}+\frac{a_r}{n}
\le \frac{ma_q}{mq}+\frac{C_q}{n}
= \frac{a_q}{q}+\frac{C_q}{n}.</math>

Taking the limit superior as <math>n\to\infty</math>, we obtain <math>\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \frac{a_q}{q}.</math>

Since <math>q</math> was arbitrary, this holds for all <math>q</math>, and therefore

<math>\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}\le \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

Combining the inequalities, we conclude that

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}=\inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

∎

== Examples ==
=== Square root ===
Define a sequence <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> by, for all <math>n\in\N</math>,

<math>a_n:=n+\sqrt{n}.</math>

One can show that this sequence is subadditive, since for all <math>n,m\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{n+m}=n+m+\sqrt{n+m}
\le n+m+\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m}
= a_n+a_m.</math>

Indeed,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{n+\sqrt{n}}{n}
= 1.</math>

=== Integer value ===
Let <math>0<c\in\R</math>. Define a sequence <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> by, for all <math>n\in\N</math>,

<math>a_n:=\lceil cn\rceil,</math>

where <math>\lceil\cdot\rceil</math> denotes the [[ceiling function]]. The sequence is subadditive, since for all <math>n,m\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{n+m}
= \lceil c(n+m)\rceil
= \lceil cn+cm\rceil
\le \lceil cn\rceil+\lceil cm\rceil
= a_n+a_m.</math>

Indeed,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{\lceil cn\rceil}{n}
= c.</math>

== Corollaries ==
=== Superadditive sequences ===
A sequence of real numbers <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> is called '''superadditive''' if and only if for all <math>m,n\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{n+m}\ge a_n+a_m.</math>

Using Fekete's lemma, one can show that for every superadditive sequence,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://planetmath.org/feketessubadditivelemma
 |title=Fekete’s subadditive lemma |website=planetmath.org |access-date=9 February 2026}}</ref>

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \sup_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

That is, the sequence <math>\frac{a_n}{n}</math> converges to its [[supremum]]. As in the subadditive case, this supremum may be <math>\infty</math>.

The proof follows by applying Fekete's lemma to the sequence <math>b_n:=-a_n</math>.

=== Submultiplicative sequences ===
A sequence of real numbers <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> is called '''submultiplicative''' if and only if for all <math>m,n\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{n+m}\le a_na_m.</math>

Using Fekete's lemma, one can show that for every submultiplicative sequence with positive terms,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{a_n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\sqrt[n]{a_n}.</math>

The proof follows by applying Fekete's lemma to the sequence <math>b_n:=\ln a_n</math>, where <math>\ln</math> denotes the [[natural logarithm]].

Note that since Fekete's lemma for submultiplicative sequences applies only to positive sequences, the infimum is necessarily finite and nonnegative. This fact has important applications, for example:

* Any [[power series]] whose coefficients have [[absolute value]]s forming a submultiplicative sequence has a positive [[radius of convergence]] (the [[Cauchy–Hadamard theorem]]).

* Every [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattice]] admits a [[connective constant]] describing the growth rate of the number of possible [[self-avoiding walk]]s.

=== Almost subadditive sequence ===
Let <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty</math> be a sequence of real numbers for which there exists <math>C\in\R</math> such that for all <math>m,n\in\N</math>,

<math>a_{n+m}\le a_n+a_m+C.</math>

Such a sequence is called '''almost subadditive'''. Then,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n+C}{n}.</math>

==== Proof ====
Define a new sequence <math>b_n:=a_n+C</math>. It is subadditive, since

<math>b_{n+m}
= a_{n+m}+C
\le a_n+a_m+C+C
= b_n+b_m.</math>

Therefore,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{b_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n+C}{n}.</math>

On the other hand,

<math>\left|\frac{b_n}{n}-\frac{a_n}{n}\right|
= \frac{C}{n}\to 0,</math>

so the two sequences have the same limit. Hence,

<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}
= \inf_{n\in\N}\frac{a_n+C}{n}.</math>

∎
